results.content: # uncertainty-calibration 0.1.4. Utilities to calibrate model uncertainties and measure calibration. # Uncertainty Calibration Library. This repository contains library code to measure the calibration error of models, including confidence intervals computed by Bootstrap resampling, and code to recalibrate models. Our functions estimate the calibration error and ECE more accurately than prior "plugin" estimators and we provide Bootstrap confidence intervals. See Verified Uncertainty Calibration for more details. Motivating example for uncertainty calibration: Calster and Vickers 2015 train a random forest that takes in features such as tumor size and presence of teratoma, and tries to predict the probability a patient has testicular cancer. Calibration is a popular way to measure the quality of a model's uncertainties, and recalibration is a way to take an existing model and correct its uncertainties to make them better. This library focuses on calibration for classification tasks. Measuring the calibration error of a model is as simple as:. Our library makes it very easy to measure confidence intervals on the calibration error as well, using bootstrap resamples. ## Advanced: ECE, Debiasing, and Top-Label Calibration Error. By default, our library measure per-class, root-mean-squared calibration error, and uses the techniques in Verified Uncertainty Calibration to accurately estimate the calibration error. However, we also support measuring the ECE (Guo et al) and using older, less accurate, ways of estimating the calibration error. get_top_calibration_error(model_probs, labels, p = 1). Multiclass calibration vs ECE / Top-label: When measuring the calibration error of a multiclass model, we can measure the calibration error of all classes (per-class calibration error), or of the top prediction. ## Verified Uncertainty Calibration paper. This repository also contains code for the NeurIPS 2019 (Spotlight) paper Verified Uncertainty Calibration. * The calibration error of methods like Platt scaling and temperature scaling are typically underestimated, and cannot be easily measured. * We propose an efficient recalibration method where the calibration error can be measured. * Experiments showing the debiased estimator can estimate calibration error with fewer samples than standard estimator (Section 5) Running each experiment saves plots in the corresponding folder in saved\_files. uncertainty-calibration-0..gz (15.9 kB view details). results.content: > By definition, **We say that a model is well calibrated when a prediction of a class with confidence p is correct 100p % of the time.**. * If we rely on the model’s prediction (say the probability score for the classification model) to make the decision, they need to be calibrated. Proper scoring rules like the Brier score and negative log-likelihood provide a measure of the calibration and accuracy of probabilistic predictions, The lower values of such metrics encourage well-calibrated and accurate probabilistic predictions. Calibration error metrics give a scalar value that quantifies the miscalibration by computing the difference between true confidence and predicted confidence. 1. ***Not computing calibration across all predictions:*** ECE is computed using only the predicted class probability (for 3-class prediction [0.1,0.75,0.05], the ECE will be computed for prob of class 1 which is 0.75) The metrics do not assess how accurate the model is for other K-1 class’s prediction. results.content: # Bootstrapped confidence intervals for performance metrics of predictive models. In the usual scenario with bootstrapped confidence intervals for a metric, the model is retrained on a number of bootstrap samples and evaluated on the corresponding remaining parts. Now, if you set up is that you have a training set that is used to build your model, and once that model is finalized its performance is evaluated with with a properly independent test set. In that case, as the model is fixed, we need to account only for the variance uncertainty due to the limited number of tested cases - as always, if the performance estimate is based on measuring more cases, the uncertainty will be lower. ## Resampling validation: Cross Validation, Set Validation, Out-Of-Bootstrap & Co. Resampling validation takes so-called surrogate models trained on a subset of the data at hand and tests them with the respective cases not used for that surrogate model's training. This is typically done for many surrogate models, and the test results are pooled and used as *approximation* for the performance of the final model which is trained with the same algorithm but on the whole data set. In that case, I use cross validation (low but pessimistic bias) and can then say that my confidence interval will be a bit too conservative - which in this case is far more acceptable than a possibly overoptimistic estimate. But what we want is the distribution of the figure of merit that pools both sources: $n\_t$ tested independent cases and $n\_b$ surrogate models. While I've not quite finished thinking though this, at the moment I bootstrap both $n\_b$ out of $n\_b$ surrogate models and $n\_t$ out of $n\_t$ test cases to construct my distribution for the figure of merit. \* As opposed to: a model trained with this training algorithm on *a* data set (not *this* data set) of size $n$ of this general population => in that case, a proper estimate of the variance will need multiple data sets, resampling validation cannot estimate it, see Bengio, Y. So if you want to get CI using bootstrap, then you don't need to refit the model many times, you just bootstrap the errors on the test set.

results.content: Advanced Methods and Metrics for ML Model Evaluation Advanced Methods and Metrics for ML Model Evaluation Elevate Your Models with Cutting‑Edge Evaluation Techniques Sarah Lee AI generated 6 min read· April 19, 2025 _Explore advanced evaluation methods—from cross‑validation variants to calibration and uncertainty estimation—to rigorously assess ML models._ 1. Model Calibration and Reliability 4. Conclusion and Further Reading Machine learning practitioners often default to metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and ROC‑AUC for model evaluation. Advanced evaluation methods dig deeper: they quantify model reliability, robustness, and interpretability. In this article, we cover: * Why single train/test splits and basic metrics fall short * Cross‑validation variants for robust performance estimates * Calibration techniques to ensure probabilistic predictions are trustworthy * Methods for quantifying uncertainty and confidence in predictions * Explainable metrics that diagnose model errors and biases * Common pitfalls encountered in production systems Whether you’re a data scientist fine‑tuning hyperparameters or an ML engineer monitoring models in production, these techniques will help you build more dependable and transparent systems. ### Need for Robust Validation Strategies * Employ multiple splits or more sophisticated cross‑validation (CV) * Report confidence intervals, not just point estimates * Combine evaluation with domain‑specific business metrics (e.g., cost, revenue impact) 2. ### Common Variants ### Nested Cross‑Validation for Hyperparameter Tuning When you perform model selection (e.g., grid search) inside CV, there’s a risk of optimistically biased performance estimates. 4. Uncertainty Estimation in Predictions Accurate point estimates are nice, but quantifying **how uncertain** a model is can be critical for risk‑sensitive tasks. ### Bootstrapping and Ensemble Methods * **Bootstrap aggregating (Bagging)**: Train multiple models on bootstrap samples and measure variability in predictions. * **Deep Ensembles**: Independently trained neural networks whose output variance approximates model uncertainty (Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017). * **Detection**: Monitor performance metrics in production; use drift detection tests (e.g., ADWIN). ### Recommended Libraries and Tools * scikit‑learn: Cross‑validation, calibration, metrics * XGBoost / LightGBM: Built‑in CV and feature importance * Fairlearn, AI Fairness 360: Bias auditing * PyMC3, TensorFlow Probability: Bayesian modeling ### Next Steps for Continuous Improvement 1. By adopting these advanced methods and metrics, you’ll not only build more accurate models but also foster greater trust and transparency in your ML systems.
